chunks: What is EMI?. The question: What is electromagnetic interference (EMI)?
EMI, electromagnetic interference, is unwanted electromagnetic energy from one circuit that disturbs another.
It always has three parts: a source that makes it, a path it travels along, and a victim it upsets. The path can be wires (conducted) or open air (radiated).
Sharp, fast signal edges make the most of it, even when the circuit's clock is slow.
Think of a hair dryer making static on an AM radio. The dryer's motor is the source.
The static reaches the radio through the air and along the shared power cord, which are the two paths. The radio is the victim. Sparks that change faster make more static.
You could cure it by quieting the motor, blocking the path, or making the radio tougher.

Break any one of the three boxes and the interference stops: reduce the source (slower edges), interrupt the path (filter, shield, separate, shrink the loop) or harden the victim (lower impedance, filtering).
Conducted EMI: noise that travels along wires, power lines and shared grounds. Radiated EMI: noise that travels through the air as electric and magnetic fields.
Rise time: how quickly a signal goes from low to high. Shorter means sharper. Harmonic: a whole-number multiple of a signal's repeat frequency.
A sharp-edged repeating signal carries energy at many of them.
Common-mode current: current flowing the same direction on both wires of a cable, which makes the cable a good antenna.
A 10 megahertz clock repeats 10 million times a second. Give it a 2 nanoseconds rise time (2 billionths of a second).
The sharp edge means it still carries meaningful energy up to about 160 megahertz, and beyond.
Slow the edge to 6 nanoseconds and that point falls to about 53 megahertz, and the energy at 1 gigahertz drops by about a factor of three. The clock frequency never changed.
Only the edge speed did, which is why slowing edges is a common first fix. That is the whole idea: EMI comes from edges and currents, not from clock speed alone.
"EMI is unwanted electromagnetic energy that disturbs a circuit.
It has a source, a coupling path and a victim, it can be conducted along wires and grounds or radiated through the air, and it's made of differential-mode and common-mode currents.

On a PCB, radiation mostly comes from current loops and from common-mode current on cables, driven by fast edges: the harmonics extend to about 1 over pi times the rise time, far above the clock frequency.
So edge rate, loop area and return paths are what I control."
